front.title: PACE: Protocol for Agent Communication Exchange

abstract.t: This document defines the Protocol for Agent Communication Exchange (PACE), a session protocol for communication between AI agents and between agents and tools over Media over QUIC Transport (MOQT). PACE provides session lifecycle management, multi-modal data exchange (real-time media, chat, tool calls, file transfers), agent identity verification, and delegated authorization — all within a unified publish/subscribe transport that supports point-to-point and point-to-multipoint topologies.

The protocol maps agent communication patterns onto MOQT primitives, leveraging MOQT's relay infrastructure for scalable fan-out, priority-based delivery, and graceful recovery from network failures through relay caching and QUIC connection migration.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: AI agents are autonomous, adaptive intelligent software systems that use AI models to complete specific tasks. These agents interact via chat or voice, making decisions, executing actions, and communicating with other agents and tools independently. As agent-to-agent and agent-to-tool communication expands across the Internet, reliable interoperability across platforms and vendors becomes critical.
The AI agent ecosystem presents unique communication requirements that existing transport protocols do not fully address:

dd.t: Agents may need to be authenticated independently of the users they represent. Verifiable agent identity enables independent revocation, scoped permissions, and auditability of agent-initiated actions.

Agents have specialized capabilities enhanced through collaboration. This raises considerations for selecting agents and tools, initiating communication, and maintaining interactions across network boundaries.

Agent interactions can be long-lived, utilize significant amounts of context across various modes (text, audio, video), and require very low latency. This introduces considerations around reliability, transport session management, and efficient data transport.
Protecting data over untrusted networks requires mechanisms for identity verification, confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, and delegated authorization across AI agent chains.

section.t: This document defines the Protocol for Agent Communication Exchange (PACE), which addresses these requirements by providing a session layer over Media over QUIC Transport (MOQT) . PACE enables diverse agent protocols to leverage MOQT's real-time streaming capabilities, built-in prioritization, scalable relay infrastructure, and efficient multiplexing over QUIC.

section.name: Design Goals
section.t: PACE is designed to meet the following objectives:

list.t: Session Lifecycle Management: Provide timed session management (short or long-lived) covering establishment, update, context handling, and termination.
Multi-Modal Data Exchange: Support concurrent exchange of real-time data (voice/video), semi-real-time data (chat/streaming text), and non-real-time data (tool calls/file transfers).
Scalable and Reliable: Enable highly scalable session management that survives network and server failures with graceful recovery.
Flexible Topologies: Support point-to-point and point-to-multipoint communication patterns through relay infrastructure.
Agent Identity and Authorization: Provide mechanisms for agent authentication independent of user identity, with delegated authorization and fine-grained behavioral scopes.
Protocol Agnostic: Serve as a session substrate usable by application-layer protocols (A2A, MCP, and others) with appropriate layering and extension points.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.name: Architecture Overview
section.t: illustrates the overall PACE architecture, showing how the session protocol layers over MOQT and QUIC, and how application protocols integrate through the extension framework.

section.name: MOQT as Session Substrate
section.t: Media over QUIC Transport (MOQT) is a publish/subscribe protocol built on QUIC that delivers low-latency, highly-scalable message distribution. MOQT decouples publishers from subscribers through intermediary relay infrastructure, enabling efficient fan-out to many consumers without requiring direct connections between endpoints.
MOQT provides several properties essential for agent communication:

list.t: Named Data Addressing: Content is addressed by hierarchical namespace tuples rather than endpoint locations, enabling location-independent data retrieval and natural caching
Application Layer Multicast: Relay infrastructure provides multicast-like fan-out without requiring network-layer multicast, making one-to-many distribution practical across the public Internet
Low Latency: QUIC's 0-RTT connection establishment, stream multiplexing to prevent head-of-line blocking, and priority-based delivery (0-255 scale) ensure time-critical messages are transmitted first
High Scalability: Publishers connect once to a relay which fans out to all subscribers; hierarchical relay networks distribute load across geographic regions
Fault Tolerance: Relay redundancy enables failover without disrupting active sessions; object caching at relays enables recovery from transient disconnections

section.t: illustrates the relay architecture that enables PACE's scalability and reliability properties.

section.name: Session Management
section.t: An PACE session represents a logical communication context between two or more agents. Sessions are the fundamental unit of interaction, providing lifetime management, context preservation, and failure recovery.

section.name: Session Lifecycle
section.t: Sessions progress through defined states:

dd.t: No session exists. Agent is available to initiate or accept sessions.
Session establishment in progress. Capability negotiation and authentication are being performed.
Session is established and data exchange is occurring. Sessions can be updated (renegotiate capabilities, add participants) while active.
Session is temporarily inactive but state is preserved. The session may be resumed without full re-establishment. Sessions automatically transition to CLOSED after a configurable timeout.
Session has terminated. Resources are released and state is cleaned up.

section.name: Session Establishment
section.t: Session establishment combines MOQT connection setup with PACE-specific negotiation of session parameters, agent identity, and capabilities.

figure.title: Session Establishment
figure.artwork:
Session Establishment Flow:
Agent A MOQT Relay Agent B │ │ │ │── QUIC/WebTransport Connect ────▶│ │ │◀── Connection Established ───────│ │ │ │ │ │── MOQT CLIENT_SETUP ───────────▶│ │ │◀── MOQT SERVER_SETUP ───────────│ │ │ │ │ │── PUBLISH_NAMESPACE ────────────▶│ │ │ (pace/{session}/ctrl/agent-a) │ │ │ │ │ │── SESSION_INIT ─────────────────▶│── SESSION_INIT ───────────────▶│ │ (identity, capabilities, │ (forwarded) │ │ requested modalities, │ │ │ session parameters) │ │ │ │ │ │ │◀── SESSION_ACCEPT ─────────────│ │◀── SESSION_ACCEPT ──────────────│ (identity, capabilities, │ │ (negotiated params) │ accepted modalities) │ │ │ │ │◀═══════ Session ACTIVE ════════▶│◀═══════════════════════════════▶│

section.t: During session establishment, agents exchange the following information:

list.t: session-id: Globally unique session identifier (UUID)
session-type: Short-lived (bounded duration) or long-lived (indefinite)
session-timeout: Maximum idle duration before automatic termination
max-participants: Maximum number of agents in the session
supported-modalities: Bitmask of data modalities the agent can handle

section.name: MOQT Setup Extensions
section.t: PACE defines the following MOQT setup parameters negotiated during CLIENT_SETUP/SERVER_SETUP:

texttable.c: Agent identity token or certificate reference

section.name: Timed Sessions
section.t: PACE supports both short-lived and long-lived sessions to accommodate different agent interaction patterns:

dd.t: Bounded duration sessions for discrete operations such as a single tool invocation or query. The session has a defined maximum lifetime and automatically terminates upon completion or timeout. Optimized for low-overhead interactions.

Indefinite sessions for ongoing collaboration, monitoring, or persistent agent relationships. These sessions survive idle periods through the SUSPENDED state and can be resumed without full re-establishment. Suitable for complex multi-step tasks, ongoing advisory relationships, or persistent tool connections.

section.t: Session timing is governed by the session-timeout parameter, which defines the maximum idle period before automatic transition to CLOSED. Agents MAY send keepalive messages to prevent timeout during periods of inactivity.

section.name: Session Update
section.t: Active sessions can be updated to renegotiate parameters without terminating the session:

list.t: Adding or removing data modalities
Adjusting priority mappings
Adding participants (transitioning from point-to-point to multipoint)
Updating authorization scopes
Extending session timeout

section.t: Updates are performed by publishing a SESSION_UPDATE message on the session control track. All participants MUST acknowledge the update before new parameters take effect.

section.name: Session Recovery
section.t: PACE provides graceful recovery from network and server failures through multiple mechanisms:

dd.t: QUIC's connection ID mechanism allows sessions to survive network path changes (e.g., WiFi to cellular) without re-establishing the MOQT session.
MOQT relays cache recent objects, allowing agents that reconnect after transient disconnections to receive missed messages from cache without requiring the peer to retransmit.
Agents that experience prolonged disconnections can resume SUSPENDED sessions by re-authenticating and providing the session-id. The relay provides cached context from the point of disconnection.
Agents SHOULD periodically publish session state checkpoints on a dedicated state track. These checkpoints enable recovery of session context after relay failures.

figure.title: Session Recovery via Relay Caching
figure.artwork:
Session Recovery Flow:
Agent A MOQT Relay Agent B │ │ │ │══ ACTIVE SESSION ═══▶│◀═════════════════════│ │ │ │ ╳ (network failure) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ (relay caches │ │ │ recent objects) │ │ │ │ │── QUIC Reconnect ──▶│ │ │── SESSION_RESUME ───▶│ │ │ (session-id, last │ │ │ received seq) │ │ │ │ │ │◀── Cached Objects ───│ (catch-up from │ │ (missed messages) │ cache) │ │ │ │ │══ SESSION RESUMED ══▶│◀═════════════════════│

section.name: Session Termination
section.t: Sessions are terminated explicitly via SESSION_CLOSE or implicitly via timeout. Upon termination:

list.t: All active subscriptions are cancelled
Pending operations receive cancellation notifications
Session state and cached objects are retained for a configurable grace period to handle in-flight messages
After the grace period, all session resources are released

section.name: Agent Identity Model
section.t: PACE defines an identity model where agents are authenticated independently of the users they represent. This separation enables:

list.t: Independent revocation of agent credentials without affecting user accounts
Scoped permissions specific to agent capabilities
Auditability of agent-initiated actions distinct from user actions
Delegation chains where agents act on behalf of other agents

section.name: Agent Identity Token
section.t: Each agent presents an identity token during session establishment. The token contains:

figure.title: Agent Identity Token Structure
figure.artwork:
Agent Identity Token Structure:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Token Header │ │ Algorithm │ Token Type │ Key ID │ ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Token Claims │ │ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ agent-id: Globally unique agent identifier │ │ │ │ issuer: Identity provider that issued the token │ │ │ │ subject: User or organization the agent serves │ │ │ │ capabilities: Agent capability descriptors │ │ │ │ scopes: Authorized operation scopes │ │ │ │ issued-at: Token issuance timestamp │ │ │ │ expires-at: Token expiration timestamp │ │ │ │ delegation-chain: Parent agent references │ │ │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Signature │ │ Cryptographic signature from issuing authority │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

section.t: The token format is based on JWT with agent-specific claims.

section.name: Delegation Chains
section.t: When an agent acts on behalf of another agent (e.g., a sub-agent invoked to handle a specialized task), the identity token includes a delegation chain that traces the authorization path:

figure.artwork:
Delegation Chain Example:
User "alice" → Agent "coordinator" → Agent "researcher" → Tool "web-search"
Each agent's token contains: delegation-chain: [ { agent: "coordinator", scope: "research.execute", granted-by: "alice" }, { agent: "researcher", scope: "web.search", granted-by: "coordinator" } ]

section.t: Receiving agents and tools can verify the complete delegation chain to ensure each link in the chain has appropriate authorization.

section.name: Agent Discovery
section.t: PACE provides in-band agent discovery through MOQT's namespace operations, enabling agents to find and evaluate potential collaborators within a session context.

section.name: Discovery Protocol
section.t: Agents advertise their presence using PUBLISH_NAMESPACE and discover others using SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE:

figure.title: Agent Discovery via MOQT Namespace Operations
figure.artwork:
Agent Discovery Flow:
Agent A MOQT Relay Agent B │ │ │ │─ SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE ──────▶│ │ │ (pace/{session}/discovery) │ │ │ │◀─ SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE ──────│ │ │ (pace/{session}/discovery) │ │ │ │ │─ PUBLISH_NAMESPACE ────────▶│ │ │ (pace/{session}/discovery/ │ │ │ agent-a) │ │ │ │─ NAMESPACE ────────────────▶│ │ │ (agent-a available) │ │ │ │ │ │◀─ PUBLISH_NAMESPACE ────────│ │ │ (pace/{session}/discovery/ │ │ │ agent-b) │ │◀─ NAMESPACE ────────────────│ │ │ (agent-b available) │ │ │ │ │ │─ SUBSCRIBE ────────────────▶│─ SUBSCRIBE ────────────────▶│ │ (agent-b/capability-card) │ │ │◀─ OBJECT (Agent Card) ──────│◀─ OBJECT (Agent Card) ──────│

section.name: Agent Capability Card
section.t: Each agent publishes a capability card as an MOQT object on its discovery track. The card advertises the agent's identity, capabilities, supported modalities, and connection parameters:

section.name: Multi-Modal Data Exchange
section.t: PACE supports concurrent exchange of multiple data modalities within a single session, each with appropriate quality of service. This enables agents to simultaneously conduct text-based reasoning, stream audio/video, invoke tools, and transfer files.

section.t: PACE defines the following data modality classes:

section.name: Channel Architecture
section.t: Each modality is mapped to dedicated MOQT tracks (channels) within the session namespace. Channels provide isolation between modalities while sharing the same session context and authorization.

figure.title: Multi-Modal Channel Layout
figure.artwork:
Multi-Modal Channel Layout:
Session Namespace: pace/{session-id}/{agent-id}/
├── ctrl/ (Session control) │ ├── session Track: session lifecycle messages │ └── auth Track: authorization updates │ ├── rt/ (Real-time modalities) │ ├── audio Track: voice stream │ ├── video Track: video stream │ └── screen Track: screen share │ ├── chat/ (Semi-real-time) │ ├── {conversation-id} Track: chat messages │ └── {stream-id} Track: streaming LLM output │ ├── ops/ (Non-real-time operations) │ ├── request Track: outbound requests │ ├── response Track: responses │ └── {operation-id} Track: operation-specific data │ ├── data/ (Bulk data) │ ├── {transfer-id} Track: file transfers │ └── context Track: context/memory exchange │ └── discovery/ (Agent discovery) └── capability-card Track: agent card

section.name: Priority and Quality of Service
section.t: MOQT's 0-255 priority scale enables differentiated treatment of messages based on their urgency and modality. PACE defines the following priority tiers:

section.name: Group Order
section.t: MOQT Group Order controls delivery sequencing within a track:

list.t: Real-time media: Descending order (newest first, drop stale frames)
Chat/streaming text: Ascending order (preserve message sequence)
Operations: Ascending order (preserve execution order)
Bulk transfers: Ascending order (sequential chunk delivery)

section.name: Request/Response Pattern
section.t: Request/response interactions use coordinated publish and subscribe operations through the MOQT relay:

figure.title: Request/Response Pattern
figure.artwork:
Request/Response Flow:
Client Agent MOQT Relay Server Agent │ │ │ │── PUBLISH ────────────▶│── forward ─────────────▶│ │ (ops/request) │ │ │ Object: { │ │ │ req-id, method, │ │ │ params, auth-token │ │ │ } │ │ │ │ │ │── SUBSCRIBE ──────────▶│ │ │ (ops/response/{id}) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ [Server processes] │ │ │ │ │ │◀── PUBLISH ─────────────│ │ │ (ops/response/{id}) │ │◀── OBJECT ─────────────│ │ │ (Response payload) │ │

section.name: Streaming Pattern
section.t: Long-running operations produce incremental results as a stream of MOQT objects organized into groups representing execution phases:

figure.title: Streaming Operation with Groups
figure.artwork:
Streaming Operation Flow:
Client MOQT Relay Server │ │ │ │── SUBSCRIBE ────────────▶│── SUBSCRIBE ────────────▶│ │ (ops/{operation-id}) │ │ │ │ │ │ │ [Group 0: Init] │ │◀── Status: "started" ────│◀── Object 0 ────────────│ │ │ │ │ │ [Group 1: Progress] │ │◀── Data: partial ────────│◀── Object 0 ────────────│ │◀── Data: more ───────────│◀── Object 1 ────────────│ │ │ │ │ │ [Group 2: Complete] │ │◀── Data: final ──────────│◀── Object 0 ────────────│ │◀── Status: "done" ───────│◀── Object 1 ────────────│ │ │ │ │── UNSUBSCRIBE ──────────▶│── UNSUBSCRIBE ──────────▶│

section.t: Groups serve as synchronization points. The server advances to a new group when transitioning between execution phases. Late-joining subscribers receive the latest complete group from relay cache.

section.name: Real-Time Media Exchange
section.t: For voice and video communication between agents (or between agents and humans), PACE maps media streams to dedicated real-time tracks with appropriate priority and delivery semantics:

list.t: Audio frames are published as individual MOQT objects with descending group order (newest-first delivery for real-time playback)
Video frames use group-based organization where each group represents a decodable unit (e.g., GOP)
MOQT's priority mechanism ensures media frames preempt lower-priority data when bandwidth is constrained

section.name: Communication Topologies
section.t: PACE supports multiple communication topologies through MOQT's relay infrastructure.

section.name: Point-to-Point
section.t: Direct communication between two agents through a relay:

figure.artwork:
Point-to-Point:
Agent A ──────▶ Relay ──────▶ Agent B ◀────── ◀──────

section.t: This is the simplest topology, used for tool invocation, simple task delegation, and bilateral collaboration.

section.name: Point-to-Multipoint (Fan-Out)
section.t: One agent publishes to multiple subscribers through relay fan-out:

figure.artwork:
Point-to-Multipoint:
┌──▶ Agent B (subscriber) │ Agent A ──▶ Relay ─────┼──▶ Agent C (subscriber) (publisher) │ └──▶ Agent D (subscriber)

section.t: This topology enables broadcast notifications, shared context distribution, and one-to-many task delegation where multiple agents observe the same operation.

section.name: Multi-Party Collaboration
section.t: Multiple agents publish and subscribe within a shared session, enabling group collaboration:

figure.artwork:
Multi-Party:
Agent A ◀──┐ ┌──▶ Agent A │ │ Agent B ◀──┼─ Relay ─┼──▶ Agent B │ │ Agent C ◀──┘ └──▶ Agent C
(All agents publish and subscribe to shared tracks)

section.t: Multi-party sessions use MOQT namespace operations to manage participant membership. Each participant publishes to their own tracks and subscribes to relevant tracks from other participants.

section.name: Participant Management
section.t: Adding a participant to an active multi-party session:

list.t: New agent establishes MOQT connection to the relay
New agent publishes SESSION_JOIN on the session control track
Existing participants receive the join notification
Existing participants publish updated capability information
New agent subscribes to relevant tracks from other participants
Session state (participant list, shared context) is updated

section.name: Hierarchical Teams
section.t: Agents can form hierarchical structures where a coordinator delegates subtasks to specialist agents:

Each level in the hierarchy operates as a separate PACE session with its own authorization scope. The coordinator's delegation chain is extended at each level, maintaining an auditable path from the original user authorization.

section.name: Authorization Model
section.t: PACE implements a fine-grained, behavior-driven authorization model where access tokens are scoped to specific operations an agent is permitted to perform.

section.name: Behavior-Driven Scopes
section.t: Unlike traditional role-based access, PACE scopes are bound to specific agent behaviors:
Scopes can include dynamic constraints that limit the scope based on runtime context (time bounds, resource limits, geographic restrictions).

section.name: Delegated Authorization
section.t: When agents invoke other agents or tools on behalf of a user, PACE supports delegated authorization that preserves the principle of least privilege:

figure.title: Delegated Authorization
figure.artwork:
Delegated Authorization Flow:
User ──── grants scope S ────▶ Agent A │ Agent A requests sub-scope S' ⊂ S │ ▼ Token Service issues S' token for Agent B │ ▼ Agent A ── invokes with S' ──▶ Agent B │ Agent B requests S'' ⊂ S' │ ▼ Agent B ── uses S'' ──▶ Tool

section.t: Each delegation narrows the scope, ensuring downstream agents cannot exceed the permissions of their delegator. The complete delegation chain is verifiable by any participant.

section.name: Authorization Token Exchange
section.t: Authorization tokens are exchanged during session establishment and can be refreshed during active sessions without interruption:

list.t: Agent presents initial authorization token in SESSION_INIT
Receiving agent validates the token and delegation chain
If additional scopes are needed, agents negotiate via the auth control channel
Token refresh is performed proactively before expiration

section.name: Confirmation and Evidence
section.t: For high-risk operations, PACE supports confirmation requirements where an agent must present evidence that a human or authorized system has approved the action:

list.t: confirmation-required: Operation requires explicit approval
evidence-type: Type of evidence (human-approval, policy-check, mfa)
evidence-token: Cryptographic proof of confirmation

section.t: This mechanism mitigates the impact of compromised agents or hallucination-driven actions by requiring out-of-band verification for sensitive operations.

section.name: Transport Security
section.t: All PACE communication is encrypted via TLS 1.3 as provided by the underlying QUIC connection. Additionally:

list.t: Agent identity tokens are cryptographically signed and verifiable
Session control messages are integrity-protected
Relay nodes operate on encrypted traffic without access to payload content (unless explicitly authorized as trusted intermediaries)
MOQT's Common Access Token provides relay-level authorization for namespace access
Agents SHOULD minimize the context and data shared in sessions to what is necessary for the task
Session metadata (participant identities, timing, access patterns) should be protected from unauthorized observation
Long-lived sessions SHOULD support forward secrecy through periodic key rotation
Relay operators MUST NOT retain session content beyond the operationally required caching period

section.name: Namespace Organization
section.t: PACE uses MOQT's hierarchical namespace system for routing, isolation, and multiplexing of sessions and protocols.

figure.title: PACE Namespace Structure
figure.artwork:
PACE Namespace Structure:
pace / {session-id} / {agent-id} / {category} -- {track-name}
Fields: pace Protocol identifier (fixed) session-id Unique session identifier agent-id Publishing agent's identifier category Message category (ctrl, rt, chat, ops, data, discovery)
Track Name: Specific identifier within the category (e.g., request-id, stream-id, modality type)

section.name: Application Protocol Multiplexing
section.t: Multiple application protocols can coexist within a single PACE session by using protocol-specific sub-categories:
This enables agents speaking different application protocols to share the same session infrastructure while maintaining message isolation.

section.name: Relay Routing
section.t: MOQT relays route subscriptions based on namespace prefixes. The hierarchical structure enables:

list.t: Session-level routing: All traffic for a session shares a prefix
Agent-level routing: Traffic to/from specific agents is identifiable
Category-level routing: Relays can apply different policies per category (e.g., prioritize real-time, rate-limit bulk transfers)

section.name: MOQT Transport Binding Layer
section.t: This section defines the concrete MOQT transport mechanics that underpin PACE sessions. While defines session lifecycle and defines multi-modal channels, this section specifies the precise mapping of protocol messages to MOQT primitives, including connection establishment sequences, message serialization formats, and operation-to-primitive mappings.

section.name: Connection Establishment
section.t: Agents using PACE MUST establish either a native QUIC connection or a WebTransport session as defined in . For native QUIC connections, agents MUST use the ALPN value "moqt". For WebTransport, the protocol is negotiated using the "WT-Available-Protocols" mechanism as specified in .
The connection setup follows this sequence:

figure.title: MOQT Connection Establishment Sequence
figure.artwork: Agent A Agent B | | |──── QUIC/WebTransport Connection ─────────────────────▶| |◄─── Connection Established ────────────────────────────| | | |──── MOQT CLIENT_SETUP ────────────────────────────────▶| | (ALPN: "moqt", | | pace-version, agent-identity, | | supported-protocols, auth-schemes) | |◄─── MOQT SERVER_SETUP ─────────────────────────────────| | (pace-version, agent-identity, | | supported-protocols, session-capabilities) | | | |──── PUBLISH_NAMESPACE (discovery) ────────────────────▶| |◄─── PUBLISH_NAMESPACE (discovery) ─────────────────────| | | |──── Capability Card Exchange ─────────────────────────▶| |◄─── Capability Card Exchange ──────────────────────────| | | |──── SESSION_INIT ─────────────────────────────────────▶| |◄─── SESSION_ACCEPT ────────────────────────────────────| | | |◄═══ Protocol Message Exchange ════════════════════════▶|

section.t: During the MOQT setup phase, agents negotiate the PACE setup parameters defined in (pace-version, agent-identity, supported-protocols, auth-schemes, and session-capabilities) as MOQT extensions in CLIENT_SETUP and SERVER_SETUP messages.

section.name: Track Organization
section.t: Agent protocol messages are mapped to MOQT tracks using a hierarchical namespace structure as defined in . MOQT namespaces consist of 1-32 ordered tuple fields, enabling relays to route based on hierarchical prefixes.

section.name: Full Track Name Structure

figure.title: Full Track Name Structure
figure.artwork:
Full Track Name Structure:
Track Namespace (tuple fields): ┌──────────┬──────────┬────────────┬──────────────┐ │ Field 1 │ Field 2 │ Field 3 │ Field 4 │ │ protocol │ session │ agent-id │ category │ └──────────┴──────────┴────────────┴──────────────┘
Track Name: ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ action or identifier │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Example Full Track Names: pace / session-123 / agent-alice / ops/request -- req-001 pace / session-123 / agent-bob / discovery -- capability-card pace / session-123 / agent-alice / a2a/stream -- task-456 pace / session-123 / agent-alice / mcp/tools -- read-file

section.t: The first namespace field is always "pace" identifying the protocol. Subsequent fields provide session routing, agent identification, and category-based message classification as defined in .

section.name: Track Category Mechanics
section.t: Tracks are organized into categories that map to MOQT publish/subscribe operations:
Subscribers discover available tracks within a category using SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE on the category prefix, receiving NAMESPACE announcements as new tracks appear.

section.name: Message Serialization
section.t: Agent protocol messages are serialized and encapsulated within MOQT objects. Each MOQT object contains a header (managed by the MOQT layer) and a protocol-specific payload:

figure.title: MOQT Object Structure with PACE Envelope

section.t: The PACE message envelope prepends minimal framing:

list.t: version (1 byte): PACE envelope version (currently 0x01)
flags (1 byte): Message flags (0x01=compressed, 0x02=fragmented, 0x04=encrypted)
length (varint): Length of the serialized protocol message

section.t: Protocol bindings SHOULD preserve native message formats where possible to maintain compatibility with existing protocol implementations. For example, A2A messages retain their JSON-RPC 2.0 format; the PACE envelope simply wraps the serialized JSON bytes.

section.name: Operation-to-Primitive Mapping
section.t: The following table provides the complete mapping of common agent communication patterns to MOQT primitives:

texttable.c: Single request published to a track
Request with incremental data across objects
Subscribe to retrieve a specific resource
Cancel signal published to control track

section.name: Protocol Bindings
section.t: This section defines concrete protocol bindings that map application protocol semantics to the MOQT transport layer defined in . Each binding operates within PACE sessions () and uses the channel architecture defined in .

section.name: Binding Architecture
section.t: Each protocol binding defines:

list.t: Protocol Identifier: Unique string (e.g., "a2a", "mcp") used in the namespace category field
Version: Protocol version supported by the binding
Namespace Pattern: How protocol operations map to PACE namespace categories and track names
Message Serialization: Encoding of protocol messages within MOQT object payloads
Operation Mapping: Protocol operations to MOQT primitives
Priority Mapping: Protocol message types to PACE priority tiers

section.t: Different protocols use distinct namespace categories within PACE sessions:

section.name: A2A Binding
section.t: The Agent-to-Agent Protocol binding maps A2A's task delegation and collaboration semantics to MOQT primitives. This binding operates within PACE sessions using the a2a/ category prefix.

section.name: Namespace Structure
section.t: A2A uses the following namespace hierarchy within an PACE session:

figure.artwork: pace/{session-id}/{agent-id}/a2a/{subcategory} -- {track-name}

section.t: Where subcategory identifies the A2A message class:

section.t: The following table maps A2A v0.3.0 operations to MOQT primitives. The Generic Pattern column references patterns from .

section.name: Message Format
section.t: A2A messages are serialized as JSON-RPC 2.0 payloads within MOQT objects. The binding preserves A2A's native message format without transformation:

section.name: Streaming Support
section.t: A2A streaming operations (SendStreamingMessage, task subscriptions) use MOQT groups and objects following the streaming pattern in .
A2A defines two streaming event types:

dd.t: Published when task state changes. Contains task ID, current state (queued, running, completed, failed, canceled), and optional message.
Published when task produces output. Contains artifact data (text, files, structured data) with incremental or complete delivery.

section.t: The mapping to MOQT objects:

list.t: Each streaming response creates a new MOQT group
Incremental updates are individual objects within the group
TaskStatusUpdateEvent and TaskArtifactUpdateEvent map to objects
Groups represent execution phases (initialization, progress, completion)

section.name: A2A Agent Card with MOQT Extension
section.t: Per A2A v0.3.0, each agent publishes an Agent Card containing identity, capabilities, and supported operations. When operating over PACE, the card includes a moqt extension block providing MOQT-specific connectivity information:
The moqt extension fields:

list.t: relayEndpoint: Native QUIC endpoint for the MOQT relay
webTransportEndpoint: WebTransport endpoint (alternative connectivity)
namespace: Agent's PACE namespace prefix
supportedExtensions: MOQT/PACE extensions supported
maxConcurrentSubscriptions: Maximum subscriptions the agent handles
cacheTTL: Recommended cache duration for the agent card (seconds)

section.name: MCP Binding
section.t: The Model Context Protocol can be transported over PACE to enable tool and resource access for agents. The complete specification for MCP over MOQT is defined in .

section.name: Namespace Structure
section.t: MCP uses the mcp/ category prefix within PACE sessions:

figure.artwork: pace/{session-id}/{server-id}/mcp/{subcategory} -- {track-name}

section.name: Agent Skills over MOQT
section.t: defines an Agent Skills architecture (Section 6) that extends AI capabilities beyond atomic tool operations. Skills provide composed instructions for complex tasks and use progressive loading (metadata, instructions, resources) that aligns naturally with MOQT's object-based delivery, enabling efficient bandwidth utilization and aggressive caching. The specification also describes relay support (Section 5) for scalable MCP deployments, including subscription aggregation where multiple client subscriptions are consolidated into single upstream requests, and content caching strategies optimized for AI workflows.

section.name: AutoGen Binding
section.t: AutoGen is a multi-agent conversation framework that enables complex LLM applications through agent collaboration. This binding defines how AutoGen's conversation patterns map to MOQT within PACE sessions.

section.name: Namespace Structure
section.t: AutoGen uses the autogen/ category prefix:

figure.artwork: pace/{session-id}/{runtime-id}/autogen/{subcategory} -- {track-name}

section.t: Where:

list.t: session-id: PACE session identifier
runtime-id: AutoGen runtime instance identifier
subcategory: Message class within the AutoGen binding

section.name: Message Format
section.t: AutoGen messages are serialized as JSON with the following structure:

section.name: Conversation Patterns
section.t: AutoGen's conversation patterns map to MOQT as follows:

dd.t: Each agent publishes to their message track. Agents subscribe to their conversation partner's track.
A coordinator agent manages turn-taking. All agents subscribe to the coordinator's broadcast track.
Hierarchical namespaces enable nested conversations: autogen/{session}/runtime-1/outer-agent/inner-runtime/inner-agent

section.name: Generic JSON-RPC Binding
section.t: This binding provides a minimal baseline for custom agent protocols that use JSON-RPC 2.0 messaging. It serves as an extensible foundation for protocols not covered by specific bindings.

section.name: Namespace Structure
section.t: Generic protocols use the ext/ category prefix with their protocol identifier:

figure.artwork: pace/{session-id}/{agent-id}/ext/{protocol-name}/{subcategory} -- {track-name}

section.t: Where:

list.t: protocol-name: Custom protocol identifier
subcategory: Protocol-defined message class

section.name: Message Format
section.t: Messages follow standard JSON-RPC 2.0:

section.name: Extension Mechanism
section.t: Custom protocols extend this binding by:

list.t: Defining additional track subcategories
Specifying custom message schemas within the JSON-RPC params
Registering protocol-specific priorities
Adding custom metadata in MOQT extension headers

section.t: Implementations SHOULD document their extensions and MAY register them in the IANA PACE Protocol Binding Registry.

section.name: Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns
section.t: The binding layer supports common multi-agent coordination patterns. Each pattern leverages MOQT's pub/sub and relay capabilities:

section.name: Sequential Orchestration
section.t: Agents execute tasks in sequence, each passing results to the next:

figure.artwork:
Sequential Pattern:
Agent A ──result──▶ Agent B ──result──▶ Agent C │ │ │ └─ publish to ──────▶└─ subscribe + ─────▶└─ subscribe + B's request publish to publish to track C's request result track track

section.t: Each agent subscribes to its predecessor's response track and publishes to the next agent's request track. MOQT groups track pipeline stages.

section.name: Concurrent (Broadcast) Pattern
section.t: A coordinator distributes work to multiple agents simultaneously:

figure.artwork:
Concurrent Pattern:
┌──▶ Agent B (specialist) │ │ Coordinator ─────┼──▶ Agent C (specialist) (publish) │ │ └──▶ Agent D (specialist) │ ◀── all subscribe to ───┘ coordinator's result aggregation track

section.t: The coordinator publishes a single request object; MOQT relay fan-out delivers it to all subscribing specialists. Results are published back to a shared aggregation track.

section.name: Handoff Pattern
section.t: An agent transfers an active task to another agent:

figure.artwork:
Handoff Pattern:
Agent A ══task══▶ [publishes HANDOFF on ctrl track] │ ▼ Agent B subscribes to task track, receives cached context from relay, continues execution

section.t: The handoff leverages MOQT's relay caching — Agent B receives the full task context (prior groups) upon subscribing, enabling seamless continuation without explicit state transfer.

section.name: Hierarchical Teams
section.t: See for topology description. In the binding layer, hierarchical teams use nested PACE sessions where each coordinator maintains a parent session and creates child sessions for sub-task delegation. Delegation chains () ensure authorization propagates correctly through the hierarchy.

section.name: Benefits of MOQT for Agent Communication
section.t: MOQT provides significant advantages over traditional agent transports, particularly for real-time collaboration and large-scale deployments.
MOQT enables real-time agent communication through low-latency streaming, priority-based message delivery, and built-in flow control that prevents overload during high-volume interactions.

The publish/subscribe model provides scalability through one-to-many broadcasts, dynamic in-band discovery via SUBSCRIBE_NAMESPACE, and relay-based distribution that prevents connection explosion in large mesh networks.
MOQT delivers reliability and resilience via QUIC connection migration, relay caching for recovery from transient disconnections, session suspension/resumption, and graceful degradation under load.

section.name: Relay Network Architecture
section.t: PACE inherits MOQT's relay architecture for geographic distribution and load management:
Properties of the relay network:

list.t: Subscription Aggregation: Multiple subscribers to the same track result in a single upstream subscription, reducing origin load
Geographic Locality: Edge relays cache content close to subscribers, minimizing round-trip latency
Load Distribution: Hierarchical structure prevents hotspots and single points of failure
Fault Isolation: Relay failures are localized; other paths continue operating

section.name: Caching Strategy
section.t: MOQT relays implement tiered caching optimized for agent communication:
Caching enables:

list.t: Late-joining participants receive current session state
Recovery from transient disconnections without peer retransmission
Reduced load on agent endpoints through relay-served responses
Efficient multipoint distribution of shared context

section.name: Threat Model
section.t: PACE considers the following threats:

list.t: Unauthorized agents joining sessions or impersonating legitimate agents
Man-in-the-middle attacks on agent communications
Privilege escalation through delegation chain manipulation
Denial of service via excessive session creation or message flooding
Data exfiltration through compromised relay nodes
Hallucination-driven operations by compromised or malfunctioning agents
All transport is encrypted via TLS 1.3 (QUIC requirement)
Agent identity tokens are cryptographically signed with short expiry
Delegation chains are validated end-to-end at each hop
Relay authorization via MOQT Common Access Tokens restricts namespace access
Rate limiting at relay nodes prevents flooding
Confirmation requirements for high-risk operations prevent hallucination-driven damage
Session timeout and explicit termination prevent resource exhaustion

section.name: Relay Trust Model
section.t: MOQT relays are trusted for routing but NOT for content inspection. Relay operators:

list.t: MUST NOT inspect or modify message payloads
MUST enforce namespace-level access control
MUST implement rate limiting and abuse prevention
MAY cache objects for operational efficiency
MUST NOT retain cached content beyond operational necessity

section.t: For deployments requiring end-to-end confidentiality even from relay operators, agents MAY implement payload encryption above the PACE layer.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Guidelines for Writing an IANA Considerations Section in RFCs

abstract.t: Many protocols make use of points of extensibility that use constants to identify various protocol parameters. To ensure that the values in these fields do not have conflicting uses and to promote interoperability, their allocations are often coordinated by a central record keeper. For IETF protocols, that role is filled by the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

To make assignments in a given registry prudently, guidance describing the conditions under which new values should be assigned, as well as when and how modifications to existing values can be made, is needed. This document defines a framework for the documentation of these guidelines by specification authors, in order to assure that the provided guidance for the IANA Considerations is clear and addresses the various issues that are likely in the operation of a registry.
This is the third edition of this document; it obsoletes RFC 5226.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

abstract.t: This document defines the core of the QUIC transport protocol. QUIC provides applications with flow-controlled streams for structured communication, low-latency connection establishment, and network path migration. QUIC includes security measures that ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability in a range of deployment circumstances. Accompanying documents describe the integration of TLS for key negotiation, loss detection, and an exemplary congestion control algorithm.

front.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

abstract.t: This document specifies version 1.3 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol. TLS allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery.
This document updates RFCs 5705 and 6066, and obsoletes RFCs 5077, 5246, and 6961. This document also specifies new requirements for TLS 1.2 implementations.

front.title: HTTP Datagrams and the Capsule Protocol

abstract.t: This document describes HTTP Datagrams, a convention for conveying multiplexed, potentially unreliable datagrams inside an HTTP connection.

In HTTP/3, HTTP Datagrams can be sent unreliably using the QUIC DATAGRAM extension. When the QUIC DATAGRAM frame is unavailable or undesirable, HTTP Datagrams can be sent using the Capsule Protocol, which is a more general convention for conveying data in HTTP connections.
HTTP Datagrams and the Capsule Protocol are intended for use by HTTP extensions, not applications.

JSON Web Token (JWT) is a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties. The claims in a JWT are encoded as a JSON object that is used as the payload of a JSON Web Signature (JWS) structure or as the plaintext of a JSON Web Encryption (JWE) structure, enabling the claims to be digitally signed or integrity protected with a Message Authentication Code (MAC) and/or encrypted.

This specification describes an optimized expression of the semantics of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), referred to as HTTP version 2 (HTTP/2). HTTP/2 enables a more efficient use of network resources and a reduced perception of latency by introducing header field compression and allowing multiple concurrent exchanges on the same connection. It also introduces unsolicited push of representations from servers to clients.
This specification is an alternative to, but does not obsolete, the HTTP/1.1 message syntax. HTTP's existing semantics remain unchanged.

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This document describes the overall architecture of HTTP, establishes common terminology, and defines aspects of the protocol that are shared by all versions. In this definition are core protocol elements, extensibility mechanisms, and the "http" and "https" Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) schemes.
This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.
